page.title: FlexText Excel Import - Easy Interlinear Text Tool

header.tagline: Convert Excel transcriptions to FLEx interlinear texts with ease

about.title: About This Tool
about.p1: The FlexText Excel Import tool is designed to make transcription and back-translation of minority language texts easier for everyone, especially native speakers who may not be familiar with complex linguistic software.
about.p2: Instead of working directly in FLEx (Fieldworks Language Explorer), you can use a familiar Excel spreadsheet to enter your text data. Then, with a simple click, this tool converts your Excel file into a FlexText format that FLEx can import directly.

feature1.title: ✨ Easy to Use
feature1.desc: No programming knowledge required. Just fill in the Excel template and click convert.

feature2.title: 📝 Familiar Format
feature2.desc: Work in Excel, a tool most people already know and understand.

feature3.title: 🚀 Fast Conversion
feature3.desc: Convert your data to FLEx-compatible format in seconds.

ossupport.title: Operating System Support
ossupport.windows: ✅ Windows: Download the .zip, extract, and run the .exe (no installation needed)
ossupport.macos: ✅ macOS (Apple Silicon): Download the .dmg, drag the app to Applications, then right‑click → Open on first launch to bypass Gatekeeper for unsigned apps

step1.title: Download and Extract
step1.desc: Download both the Windows application (.exe) and the Excel templates (.zip). Extract the templates from the zip file to a location on your computer.

step2.title: Fill in the Template
step2.desc: Open one of the Excel templates (choose the size based on your text length). Fill in your text data following the template structure. Make sure to fill in the writing system codes at the top of the sheet to match your FLEx project. Use the "Code" value from FLEx writing system settings (not Abbreviation). See Writing System Codes.

step3.title: Convert
step3.desc: Double-click the converter application (.exe file). Select your Excel file as input, choose where to save the output, and click Convert.

step4.title: Import into FLEx
step4.desc: Open FLEx and switch to the Interlinear Text view (you must be in this view to see the import option). Then go to File → Import → Interlinear Text... and select your generated .flextext file.

step1.title: Step 1: Prepare Your Excel File
step1.li1:
Choose one of the three template sizes based on your text:
  • 80 lines: Short texts or stories
  • 200 lines: Medium-length texts
  • 1000 lines: Long texts or extended narratives
step1.li2: Open the template in Microsoft Excel or a compatible program
step1.li3:
Important: Fill in the writing system codes in the header section (top right of the sheet). These codes must match your FLEx project settings. Use the FLEx Code value from the General tab (do NOT use Abbreviation or language name). See Writing System Codes for details:
  • Vernacular writing system: Usually a 2-3 letter language code (e.g., "en", "spa", "qaa")
  • Gloss writing system: The language code for word glosses
  • Free translation writing system: The language code for free translations
step1.li4:
Enter your text data in the appropriate columns:
  • Original language text in the vernacular column
  • Word-by-word glosses in the gloss column
  • Free translations (sentence/paragraph level) in the free translation column
step1.li5: Save your completed file as an Excel workbook (.xlsx)

step2.title: Step 2: Run the Converter
step2.li2: A window will open with the converter interface
step2.li3: Select "Excel Interlinear" as the input format (should be default)
step2.li4: Click "Select input file & load" and choose your Excel file
step2.li5: Wait for the file to load (progress bar will show status)
step2.li6: Review the writing systems displayed to ensure they match your expectations
step2.li7: Select "FlexText Interlinear" as the output format
step2.li9: Choose where to save the output file (same name as input with .flextext extension is suggested)

step3.title: Step 3: Import into FLEx
step3.li2: Important: Switch to the Interlinear Text view in FLEx. The import option will not be visible if you're in another view (such as Lists, Data Notebook, or Lexicon view). Look for "Texts & Words" in the menu bar to access Interlinear Text view.
step3.li3:
Important: Before importing, configure your writing systems in FLEx:
  • Go to Tools → Configure → Writing Systems...
  • Ensure your vernacular and analysis writing systems are set up using the correct Code values (not Abbreviation)
  • Go to Tools → Configure → Interlinear... (in the Gloss or Analyze tab)
  • Set the writing systems for Word Gloss and Free Translation
  • Make sure these match the codes you used in your Excel template
step3.li7: Your text should now appear in FLEx as an interlinear text

tips.title: Tips for Success
tips.li1: Writing system codes must match exactly between your Excel file and FLEx project
tips.li2: If you don't see your text after importing, check your writing system settings in FLEx
tips.li3: The order of writing systems in FLEx's interlinear settings should match your Excel template
tips.li4: Each text/tab in FLEx has its own interlinear settings - configure them individually
tips.li5: Start with a small test file to ensure your setup is correct before converting larger texts

writingsystem.title: ⚠️ Writing System Configuration
writingsystem.intro: The most common issue users encounter is with writing system settings. FLEx requires that:
writingsystem.li1: Writing system codes in your Excel file exactly match those in your FLEx project (use the Code field; not Abbreviation)
writingsystem.li2: Writing systems must be configured in both the project-wide settings AND individual text settings
writingsystem.li3: The order of writing systems in FLEx's interlinear settings should match your template
writingsystem.symptom:
Symptom: You import a file but see nothing displayed in FLEx.
Solution: Check and adjust your writing system settings as described in the "How to Use" section above.

platform.title: 🖥️ Platform Availability
platform.macos: macOS and Linux: Currently requires Python 3.8+ and manual setup. Advanced users can run from source code following the developer instructions on GitHub.

excel.title: 📋 Excel Compatibility
excel.li1: Only works with files created from the provided templates
excel.li2: Custom Excel structures are not supported
excel.li3: Must be saved as .xlsx format (not .xls or .csv)

data.title: 📝 Data Limitations
data.li1: Complex formatting in Excel cells may not transfer correctly
data.li2: Template must be used as-is; adding or removing columns will break the converter
data.li3: Very large files (thousands of lines) may take longer to process

tech.title: 🔧 Technical Issues
tech.li1: Windows may show a security warning when running the .exe file (this is normal for unsigned applications). Click "More info" and then "Run anyway" if you trust the source.
tech.li2: Some antivirus software may flag the executable as suspicious (false positive). You may need to add an exception.

bugs.title: 🐛 Known Bugs
bugs.p: For the latest bug reports and to report new issues, please visit the GitHub Issues page.

q1.q: Q: Do I need to install anything?
q1.a: A: On Windows, no installation is required. Just download the .exe file and run it. On macOS/Linux, you'll need Python 3.8 or newer installed.

q2.q: Q: Can I use this with LibreOffice or Google Sheets?
q2.a: A: LibreOffice and Google Sheets may be able to open the templates, but they will not include the protection features designed to make sure your native speaking coworkers only enter text in the appropriate fields. Highly recommended to use Excel and not LibreOffice or Google Sheets, though as long as people very carefully put things exactly where they belong without changing the sheet layout at all and save as .xslx, it might still work.

q3.q: Q: My text doesn't show up in FLEx after importing. What's wrong?
q3.a:
A: This is almost always a writing system configuration issue. Check that:
  1. The writing system codes in your Excel file match those in your FLEx project exactly
  2. You've configured writing systems in Tools → Configure → Writing Systems...
  3. You've configured interlinear settings in Tools → Configure → Interlinear...
  4. The writing systems are in the same order in both places

q4.q: Q: What writing system codes should I use?
q4.a:
A: Use the same codes that are already set up in your FLEx project. Common examples:
  • "en" for English
  • "es" or "spa" for Spanish
  • "fr" or "fra" for French
  • Your specific language's ISO 639 code
Copy the value labeled Code (not Abbreviation) from the General tab in Tools → Configure → Writing Systems…. See Writing System Codes.

q5.q: Q: Which template size should I use?
q5.a:
A: Choose based on your text length:
  • 80 lines: Short texts, single stories, or when you're just starting
  • 200 lines: Medium texts, most common use case
  • 1000 lines: Long narratives or multiple stories in one file
You can always start with a smaller template and switch to a larger one if needed.

q6.q: Q: Can I modify the Excel template?
q6.a:
A: You can modify the content and some formatting, but do NOT:
  • Add or remove columns
  • Change the structure of the template
  • Move the writing system codes section
These changes will break the converter.

q7.q: Q: Is my language data secure?
q7.a: A: Yes. This tool runs completely on your local computer. No data is sent to the internet or any external servers. Your Excel files and converted FlexText files stay on your computer.

q8.q: Q: Can I use this tool for languages other than English?
q8.a: A: Absolutely! This tool is specifically designed for minority languages. It supports any language that FLEx supports, as long as you configure the writing system codes correctly.

q9.q: Q: I'm getting an error message. What should I do?
q9.a:
A: The converter displays error messages in the bottom panel. Common errors include:
  • "Writing system code must be 2 or 3 letters": Check the codes at the top of your Excel file
  • "File does not exist": Make sure you saved your Excel file before trying to convert
  • Loading errors: The Excel file may be corrupted or not based on the template
If you can't resolve the error, please report it on the GitHub Issues page.

q10.q: Q: Can I contribute to this project?
q10.a:
A: Yes! This is an open-source project. You can contribute by:
  • Reporting bugs or requesting features on GitHub
  • Submitting code improvements via Pull Requests
  • Helping translate documentation
  • Sharing your experience with other users
Visit the GitHub repository to get started.

page.title: Writing System Codes — FlexText Excel Import

header.title: Writing System Codes
header.tagline: These must match your FLEx project exactly

wsc.callout: Important: If the writing system codes in your Excel sheet (or those you enter in the converter) do not exactly match the codes already defined in your FLEx project, FLEx will create new writing systems and your imported data will be placed there. This leads to duplicates and a messy cleanup. Always use the exact codes from your FLEx project.

whichcode.title: Which code to use
whichcode.p:
Use the value labeled Code on the General tab of the Writing System properties.
Do not use the Abbreviation or the language name text.

wheretofind.title: Where to find it in FLEx
wheretofind.li2:
Select the relevant writing system
  • Vernacular for the baseline text
  • Analysis for Gloss and Free Translation
wheretofind.li3: Go to the General tab and copy the value in Code, immediately under the General tab (e.g., grc). DO NOT use the Language Code, Abbreviation, Language Name, or Ethnologue code (except if it happens to be identical to just plain Code).

screenshot.caption: Use the Code value (circled in the screenshot). Do not use Abbreviation or Language Name.

entercodes.title: Enter these codes in the converter
entercodes.li2: Gloss Writing System: the Analysis Code used for word glosses
entercodes.li3: Free Translation Writing System: the Analysis Code used for free translations
entercodes.note: Codes are BCP 47 tags (e.g., en, grc, es-419, or custom tags). Enter them exactly as shown in FLEx (including case).

wrongcodes.title: If you already imported with the wrong codes
wrongcodes.li2: Remove the unintended/duplicate writing systems FLEx created
